transcript:
Meeting header:
2026-05-08 15:23 UTC | Duration: 43m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jamie Lin (Redwood AE), Sanjay Rao (Redwood SE), Priya Mehta (Redwood CSM) -- Aisha Patel (Nova Eng Mgr), Tom Herrera (CTO), Lana Cho (DevOps), Miguel Santos (SRE)

Auto-generated summary: run-through of SDK quickstarts, auth options, env setup, initial sizing discussion and next steps.

00:00 Jamie Lin: hey everybody, thanks for joining, uh we have Jamie from Redwood, Sanjay our solutions engineer and Priya from customer success. How's everyone doing at Nova?
00:08 Aisha Patel: Morning, yeah all good, thanks. We have Tom on for architecture and Lana and Miguel for infra, wanted to focus on how fast we can get the SDK into our services and what the auth story looks like.
00:18 Jamie Lin: perfect, that's exactly what we planned for. Quick agenda: 1) walk through Python quickstart, 2) TypeScript example, 3) auth and env setup, 4) perf and hosting options, and 5) next steps. Sound good?
00:28 Tom Herrera: sounds great. we're particularly sensitive to PII and residency so we might need private or dedicated.
00:34 Sanjay Rao: totally, we'll cover those trade-offs. quick note — I'll paste code samples in the chat as we go, and also the quickstart repo link.

05:02 Sanjay Rao: ok opening the Python quickstart, so first step is pip install redwood-inference — or sometimes in docs we call it redwood-sdk, there's been a rename in places, so if you see either that's fine, sorry about that, docs lag.
05:15 Aisha Patel: ha, yeah we've seen that with other libs too.
05:18 Sanjay Rao: snippet — set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your environment, import redwood, then client = redwood.Client() and client.generate("prompt..."). Example:
05:30 Sanjay Rao: (code read) from redwood import Client
05:35 Sanjay Rao: client = Client(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"))
05:40 Miguel Santos: quick Q — do you recommend storing the key in env vars or use Vault? our infra prefers HashiVault.
05:46 Sanjay Rao: great question — env vars are fine for local dev and containers but for prod we do recommend rotating keys in a secret store (Vault/KV) and using short-lived tokens. We also support OIDC federation for SSO so you can mint per-service creds.
06:03 Lana Cho: how does SSO/OIDC mapping to RBAC work? we need team-based permissions and audit logs.
06:09 Sanjay Rao: we integrate with SSO providers via OIDC/SAML, map groups to roles in the console. Audit logs and token-level tracing are available — you'll get per-request metadata and a token/route cost breakdown. There is an admin role and then routes can be scoped with RBAC.

10:05 Jamie Lin: switching to TypeScript quickstart, npm i @redwood/inference (again package names in examples may vary), then import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
10:22 Jamie Lin: quick demo: sending a chat style request with streaming — you'll see chunked responses and we have SDK helpers for streaming into websockets or server-sent events.
10:39 Aisha Patel: do you have an official Node streaming example for our frontend? we want to do partial render of responses.
10:45 Jamie Lin: yes, we'll share the sample react/ssr streaming snippet in the repo.

14:17 Tom Herrera: back to hosting choices, we have 3 concerns: latency <120ms p50 for single-turn checks, cost per token, and data residency for EU. we also have bursty traffic.
14:30 Sanjay Rao: for low-latency single-turn you can go Dedicated GPU pools or Private with colocated infra. Hosted can get you close depending on model and sequence length but Dedicated gives predictable p50 and throughput. We recommend prefix/KV caching for repeated context to reduce tokens and latency.
14:50 Miguel Santos: prefix KV cache — is that the same as KV cache? our notes call it K V cache and sometimes it shows up as KVCache in logs, so just making sure.
14:59 Sanjay Rao: yes there is some variation in naming — it is the KV cache that stores key/value attention states to accelerate subsequent tokens. we also do prefix caching for repeated prompts.

18:12 Lana Cho: what about encryption and KMS? our security team requires customer-managed keys and HSM.
18:18 Sanjay Rao: we support KMS integrations — cloud KMS and external HSM via customer-managed key wrap. For Private deployments you can bring your own KMS and we can integrate with your HSM. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and SOC2 audit logs.

22:03 Aisha Patel: transcription note: sorry, I have to step away briefly. One other question — how do we do local dev to mirror the production env?
22:12 Jamie Lin: good question. recommended flow: 1) local quickstart uses a sandbox API key with limited quotas, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env, 2) run local mock server from the quickstart repo to emulate streaming and latency, 3) integration tests point to a staging Redwood endpoint with token-based creds. We'll include a docker-compose dev example.

25:50 Sanjay Rao: performance notes: based on similar finance customers, for short prompts (<=512 tokens) we suggest batch sizes 8-16 for throughput, with async streaming to keep p50 low. For higher concurrency prefer Dedicated pools with CPU-scaled routing for embeddings. I'll attach an initial spreadsheet with batch size vs latency numbers.
26:22 Tom Herrera: do you have example cost estimates? we need to model committed capacity.
26:30 Jamie Lin: yes, we'll include Dedicated tier pricing in the spreadsheet. there's usually a mixing strategy: hosted for dev and low usage, Dedicated for mission critical endpoints, and Private if residency/compliance demands it.

30:40 Miguel Santos: on network — our egress goes through corporate proxy and we have strict IP allow lists. Can we pin IPs for outbound calls to Hosted?
30:49 Sanjay Rao: you can either use IP allow list for our Hosted regions or use VPC peering for Dedicated/Private. For strict environments we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) so you control the network and no public egress.

33:16 Aisha Patel: any gotchas with SDK versioning and model pinning? we need to guarantee model version for regulatory reasons.
33:24 Sanjay Rao: the SDK is backward compatible — but we strongly recommend pinning model versions in the request and pinning runtime variants in the console. We also support immutable model version tags for canary and rollouts.

36:00 Jamie Lin: ok to recap — we'll send: 1) SDK quickstart repo (Python + Node) with docker-compose dev example, 2) streaming examples for frontend, 3) benchmark spreadsheet and Dedicated pricing, 4) security whitepaper and SOC2 docs, and 5) proposed time for VPC/private feasibility call. Anything to add?
36:18 Tom Herrera: please include an example env file and a sample of request traffic histogram so we can run cost modeling.
36:25 Jamie Lin: noted — Aisha, Lana, Miguel if you can share a week's token histogram that'd be great.

39:05 Aisha Patel: one last quick question — do you support per-request metadata tagging for audit? we need to tie model calls back to user ids for investigations.
39:12 Sanjay Rao: yes, metadata/tags are supported and captured in audit logs and traces. For Private installs logs can be shipped to your SIEM.

42:00 Jamie Lin: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and propose the next call. appreciate your time.
42:08 Tom Herrera: thanks, that was helpful.
42:12 Meeting ended.

Notes about transcript quality: some package names and product nouns were inconsistent (redwood-inference vs redwood-sdk), and KV cache sometimes transcribed inconsistently as K V cache. There was natural filler and a brief step-away.
